newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration denies Black English funds.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration denies Black English funds.

text.p: The Clinton administration said Tuesday so-called Black English, or Ebonics, should not be recognized as a foreign language and federal bilingual education funds could not be used to promote it.

"Elevating 'Black English' to the status of a language is not the way to raise standards of achievement in our schools and for our students," Education Secretary Richard Riley said in a statement that followed a California school board's decision last Wednesday to recognize Black English as a primary language for many of its black students.

Oakland Unified School District spokeswoman Darolyn Davis defended the board's policy Tuesday and said district officials were not seeking bilingual funds by recognizing Ebonics. "The district is not interested in bilingual funding," she said.

Last week's resolution by the Oakland school board called on the district to provide teacher training in Ebonics, recognize it as distinct from standard English and help black students who use Ebonics to master standard English.

"The administration's policy is that 'Ebonics' is a non-standard form of English and not a foreign language," Riley said. "It has been determined by the United States Department of Education and the Clinton Administration that the use of Federal bilingual education funds for ... 'Ebonics' is not permitted."
The Oakland school board's decision was blasted Sunday by civil rights leader Rev. Jesse Jackson, who said it would undermine black students' chances for success.

"I understand the attempt to reach out to these children, but this is an unacceptable surrender borderlining on disgrace ... It's teaching down to our children and it must never happen," Jackson said on NBC television's "Meet the Press" program.
He appealed to the school board to reverse its decision, saying black children would face much harder prospects finding jobs if they had not mastered standard English.
Oakland school officials say linguists recognize Ebonics as a distinct language with origins in the West and Niger-Congo African languages.

District educators hope the program -- which may be the first in the nation -- will help improve the performance of black students. An estimated 53 percent of Oakland's nearly 52,000 students are black and officials say they have the lowest average grade point averages in the district.
District officials said it was not clear how they would fund the program.
